findings.summary: The mnemonic is shown after the layer list but its letters do not match the layer order shown, and the full layer names are repeated on a separate line, so the same list appears twice.
findings.evidence: "Mnemonic: All People Seem To Need Data Processing" followed by "Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical"
findings.fix: Keep the L7-L1 list and the mnemonic only, and label the mnemonic as top-to-bottom. Drop the repeated name line.

findings.summary: The 'What Layering Does' bullets state three ideas as bare fragments and give no visual of the stacked layers or peer-to-peer communication.
findings.evidence: "Each layer serves the layer above it" / "Each layer talks to the same layer on the peer host"
findings.fix: Add a small two-column stack diagram of Host A and Host B with horizontal peer arrows per layer and vertical service arrows.

findings.summary: FCS is introduced as a term without ever being expanded or explained, and the cheat sheet and quiz rely on it.
findings.evidence: "L2 Data Link | MAC addressing, framing, FCS error detection | one link"
findings.fix: Expand on first use: "FCS (Frame Check Sequence): a checksum trailer the receiver uses to detect corrupted frames."

findings.summary: The L5 bullet holds several ideas with examples that are not clearly L5 protocols, and the L6 bullet packs three separate functions (encoding, encryption, compression) into one line.
findings.evidence: "L6 Presentation: encoding, encryption, compression; TLS, JPEG, ASCII/UTF-8"
findings.fix: Split into one bullet for the job and one for examples, or use a Layer | Job | Examples table like the lower layers.

findings.summary: The encapsulation flow is written as a flat list of stacked words with no arrows, so the order and which header wraps what cannot be followed at a glance. The trailer point is also repeated three times.
findings.evidence: "Data / L7-L5 / + TCP header / segment / + IP header / packet / + Eth header + FCS / frame" and "Only Data Link adds a trailer (FCS)" repeated under "Trailer" and in Interview Point
findings.fix: Draw nested boxes or a left-to-right diagram: Data -> [TCP|Data] segment -> [IP|segment] packet -> [Eth|packet|FCS] frame. State the trailer rule once.

findings.summary: The 'Interview Point' section poses questions with answers inline, which makes the page read like prose Q&A rather than scannable notes. The answers repeat earlier content.
findings.evidence: "Which layer adds a trailer? Data Link only, the FCS."
findings.fix: Replace with a short Q | A table or cut the section, since the earlier tables already cover it.

findings.summary: NAT is used to qualify the IP rule but is never defined or explained.
findings.evidence: "NAT rewrites the IP at the boundary"
findings.fix: Add one line defining NAT, for example: "NAT: a router or firewall translates private source IPs to a public IP at the network edge."

findings.summary: The TCP handshake is a flat list of labels with no direction shown, so the sequence cannot be followed as a diagram. The L6 row also lists only TLS and omits other L6 items used on page 2.
findings.fix: Render as a sequence diagram with client and server lanes and arrows labelled SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK.

findings.summary: The protocol table places TLS at L6 while the 'Common slips' note and page 2 place TLS at L5-L6 and L6 examples; TLS placement is stated inconsistently.
findings.evidence: "L6 | TLS/SSL (L5-L6, not L7)" vs page 2 "L6 Presentation: ... TLS" vs "TLS sits at L5-L6, not only L7"
findings.fix: Use one phrasing everywhere, for example 'TLS: L5-L6 (not L7)', and keep that in a single place.

findings.summary: The Addresses section crams three separate facts about MAC, IP and NAT into adjacent bare lines without a table or hop diagram.
findings.evidence: "MAC: rewritten at every hop / IP: stays end to end / NAT rewrites the IP at the boundary"
findings.fix: Add a small Host -> Router -> Server strip showing which of MAC and IP change at each hop.

findings.summary: The troubleshooting steps are a flat list of layer then hint with no ordering arrow, and the warning bullets at the end repeat points from page 4 and are not tied to any section.
findings.evidence: "L1 / cable, link light / L2 / ARP/MAC, VLAN ..." and "ping is ICMP at L3, not a TCP test / TLS is not only L7"
findings.fix: Render as a numbered bottom-up flow L1 -> L2 -> L3 -> L4 -> L7 and move the repeated slips into one 'Common slips' note.

findings.summary: The 'Remember' line says only a router splits broadcast domains, which contradicts the chapter's own VLAN caveat.
findings.evidence: "A switch splits collision domains; only a router splits broadcast domains." versus the table row "Switch | 1 per port | 1 (unless VLANs)"
findings.fix: Reword to: "A switch splits collision domains; a router (or VLANs, which need a router or L3 switch to talk to each other) splits broadcast domains."

findings.summary: The closing 'Remember' line says only a router splits broadcast domains, which contradicts the VLAN caveat taught on pages 5 and 6.
findings.evidence: "A switch splits collision domains; only a router splits broadcast domains." vs the table row "Switch | 1 per port | 1 (unless VLANs)"
findings.fix: Reword to: "A switch splits collision domains; a router (or VLANs) splits broadcast domains."

findings.summary: The cheat sheet row L7/6/5 lists firewall and load balancer as devices while the L1 row has hub and repeater, and the page's definition of firewall layer conflicts in scope with page 5 which says L3/L4 stateful up to L7.
findings.evidence: "L7/6/5 | data | — | HTTP, DNS, SMTP, SSH | firewall, load balancer" and "Firewalls and load balancers work from L4 up to L7"
findings.fix: Keep one phrase for the firewall and load balancer span and either list them only in the L4 row or note 'L4-L7' in both rows consistently.

findings.summary: The quiz answer relies on switch flooding of unknown destination MACs, which no earlier page teaches.
findings.evidence: "Unknown destination MAC: the switch floods it" (page 5 only says "Switch forwards only to the destination port")
findings.fix: Add a line on page 5 saying a switch floods a frame out all other ports when the destination MAC is not yet in the CAM table, and that this is how it learns.

findings.summary: The first answer holds multiple ideas in a block, and the unknown-destination flooding point appears as a stray bullet under a question about hubs and switches.
findings.evidence: "TTL also drops by 1, but it was not one of the three" and "Unknown destination MAC: the switch floods it"
findings.fix: Give each question a short answer line plus a bullet list of reasons, and attach the flooding case as an explicit third sub-case labelled for the switch.
